elements.name: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)
elements.what: Tie a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime so acquisition happens in the constructor and release happens deterministically in the destructor at scope exit.
elements.problem: Manual release paths leak resources on early returns and exceptions; RAII makes cleanup automatic and exception-safe.
elements.named_in: The C++ Programming Language - Bjarne Stroustrup (1985; term coined by Stroustrup)

elements.name: Scope Guard
elements.what: An ad-hoc RAII object that runs an arbitrary cleanup or rollback action when a scope exits, optionally dismissible on success.
elements.problem: One-off cleanup/rollback obligations (not tied to a reusable resource class) must still run on every exit path including exceptions.
elements.named_in: Generic<Programming>: Change the Way You Write Exception-Safe Code - Forever - Andrei Alexandrescu & Petru Marginean, Dr. Dobb's/CUJ (2000)

elements.name: Pimpl
elements.what: A class exposes only a pointer to a privately defined implementation object, hiding all data members and private details from the header.
elements.problem: C++ headers leak implementation detail, causing compile-time coupling and ABI fragility; pimpl decouples interface from representation.
elements.named_in: Advanced C++: Programming Styles and Idioms - James O. Coplien (1992) (as Handle/Body; 'pimpl' popularized by Herb Sutter, GotW)

elements.name: Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP)
elements.what: A class derives from a template instantiated with itself, letting the base call derived-class members at compile time.
elements.problem: Provides polymorphic-style reuse and interface injection without virtual dispatch cost; the related Barton-Nackman trick is a historical application.
elements.named_in: Curiously Recurring Template Patterns - James Coplien, C++ Report (1995)

elements.name: Type Erasure
elements.what: Wrap arbitrary concrete types satisfying an interface behind a single value type, hiding the concrete type via an internal vtable/template bridge.
elements.problem: Combines value semantics with runtime polymorphism and removes client dependencies on concrete types and inheritance hierarchies.
elements.named_in: C++ Software Design - Klaus Iglberger (2022)

elements.name: Copy-and-Swap
elements.what: Implement assignment by constructing a copy and swapping its guts with *this via a non-throwing swap, so the operation either fully succeeds or leaves the object untouched.
elements.problem: Hand-written assignment operators struggle with self-assignment and partial-failure states; copy-and-swap gives the strong exception guarantee for free.
elements.named_in: Exceptional C++ - Herb Sutter (1999)

elements.name: Rule of Three/Five/Zero
aka: rule of the big four (and a half)
elements.what: If a class defines any of destructor/copy/move special members it should deliberately define the whole set (three/five) - or own no resources directly and define none (zero).
elements.problem: Compiler-generated special members silently mismanage owned resources (double frees, slicing of ownership semantics); the rule makes ownership responsibilities explicit.
elements.named_in: C++ Core Guidelines (C.20/C.21) - Stroustrup & Sutter (living)
elements.borderline: A coding guideline about special members rather than a standalone mechanism; kept because it is the named contract governing RAII-style ownership.

elements.name: Non-Virtual Interface (NVI)
elements.what: Public interface functions are non-virtual and delegate to private/protected virtual hooks that derived classes override.
elements.problem: Separates the interface contract (invariants, pre/postconditions, instrumentation) from the customization points, keeping base-class control over how overrides are invoked.
elements.named_in: Virtuality - Herb Sutter, C/C++ Users Journal (2001)

elements.name: Policy-Based Design
elements.what: Assemble a class's behavior from small orthogonal 'policy' template parameters, each supplying one aspect (allocation, threading, checking).
elements.problem: Monolithic classes cannot cover the combinatorial space of design choices; policies let users compose exactly the variant they need at compile time with no runtime cost.
elements.named_in: Modern C++ Design - Andrei Alexandrescu (2001)

elements.name: Mixin
elements.what: A small class providing one slice of behavior that is composed into other classes by inheritance (in C++ typically by inheriting from a template parameter) rather than used standalone.
elements.problem: Cross-cutting behaviors (counting, serialization, non-copyability) would otherwise be duplicated across unrelated hierarchies; mixins make them composable units.
elements.named_in: Mixin-Based Inheritance - Gilad Bracha & William Cook (OOPSLA 1990; term from Lisp Flavors, Moon 1986)

elements.name: Expression Templates
elements.what: Overloaded operators build compile-time expression trees instead of computing eagerly, letting whole expressions be evaluated in one fused pass.
elements.problem: Naive operator overloading on vectors/matrices creates temporaries per operation; expression templates eliminate temporaries and enable loop fusion in numeric libraries.
elements.named_in: Expression Templates - Todd Veldhuizen, C++ Report (1995)

elements.name: Small Buffer Optimization
elements.what: A container or wrapper embeds a small fixed-size buffer inside itself and only falls back to heap allocation when contents exceed it.
elements.problem: Heap allocation dominates cost for typically-small payloads (short strings, small callables); inline storage removes the allocation and improves locality.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living)

elements.name: Tag Dispatching
elements.what: Select among overloads at compile time by passing an extra empty 'tag' type argument that encodes a property of the inputs.
elements.problem: Different implementations are optimal for different type categories (e.g. iterator strength); tags route the call without runtime branching or specialization sprawl.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living)
elements.borderline: Compile-time overload-selection plumbing; near the raw-language floor but named, recurring, and a standard-library house technique.

elements.name: Copy-on-Write
elements.what: Share one representation among logical copies and physically copy only when a writer is about to mutate shared state.
elements.problem: Eager deep copies waste time and memory when most copies are never modified; COW defers the cost to actual mutation (with well-known multithreading hazards).
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); the general mechanism is classical OS vocabulary (fork COW pages)

elements.name: SFINAE
aka: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
elements.what: Exploit the rule that invalid template-argument substitution removes a candidate from overload resolution to enable/disable overloads based on type properties.
elements.problem: Generic code must choose implementations by capability of the instantiating types; SFINAE gives compile-time introspection and constraint before language-level concepts existed.
elements.named_in: C++ Templates: The Complete Guide - Vandevoorde & Josuttis (2002; acronym coined here)

elements.name: Traits Class
elements.what: A template that associates compile-time information (types, constants, operations) with a type non-intrusively, specialized per type.
elements.problem: Generic code needs per-type metadata and adaptation points without modifying the types themselves; traits externalize that mapping.
elements.named_in: Traits: a new and useful template technique - Nathan Myers, C++ Report (1995)

elements.name: Nifty Counter
elements.what: A per-translation-unit static counter object ensures a shared static resource (e.g. std::cout) is initialized before first use and destroyed after last use across translation units.
elements.problem: C++ gives no cross-translation-unit ordering for static initialization (the static initialization order fiasco); the counter forces correct init/teardown ordering.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living)

elements.name: Construct On First Use
elements.what: Access a static object only through a function that holds it as a function-local static, so it is constructed on the first call.
elements.problem: Avoids the static initialization order fiasco by making initialization demand-driven; since C++11 the construction is also thread-safe.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); popularized by the C++ FAQ (Cline) and Effective C++ (Meyers)

elements.name: Erase-Remove
elements.what: Combine std::remove/remove_if (which compacts kept elements) with container erase to actually delete matching elements from a sequence container.
elements.problem: STL algorithms cannot change container size; the two-step idiom is the established way to physically delete elements without quadratic cost.
elements.named_in: Effective STL - Scott Meyers (2001)
elements.borderline: A micro container-usage idiom rather than a design mechanism; kept as a canonical named C++ idiom (now std::erase_if).

elements.name: Named Parameter Idiom
elements.what: Replace long positional parameter lists with a parameter object whose chained setter calls name each argument, passed to the real function.
elements.problem: Calls with many defaulted positional arguments are unreadable and error-prone in languages without named arguments; the idiom simulates them.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); classical C++ FAQ (Cline) entry

elements.name: Empty Base Optimization (EBO)
elements.what: Inherit from (rather than store) an empty policy/allocator class so it occupies zero bytes in the derived object's layout.
elements.problem: Stateless components stored as members still cost at least one byte plus padding; EBO removes that overhead in size-sensitive generic code.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); 'The Empty Member C++ Optimization' - Nathan Myers, Dr. Dobb's (1997)
elements.borderline: Object-layout micro-optimization near the compiler floor; kept because it is named, recurring, and shapes generic-library design.

elements.name: Virtual Constructor
elements.what: Provide virtual clone()/create() members so code can copy or construct objects polymorphically through a base pointer.
elements.problem: Constructors cannot be virtual, so copying an object of unknown dynamic type needs an explicit polymorphic hook; this is the C++ realization of GoF Prototype.
elements.named_in: Advanced C++: Programming Styles and Idioms - James O. Coplien (1992)

elements.name: Function Object
elements.what: An object overloading the call operator so it can be invoked like a function while carrying state and being inlinable through templates.
elements.problem: Plain function pointers carry no state and defeat inlining in generic algorithms; function objects give stateful, zero-overhead callables.
elements.named_in: Advanced C++: Programming Styles and Idioms - James O. Coplien (1992; 'functor')

elements.name: Counted Body
elements.what: A handle/body pair where the body carries an embedded reference count that handles increment/decrement to share and reclaim the body.
elements.problem: Sharing a representation among handles needs deterministic reclamation without garbage collection; the embedded count makes sharing cheap and explicit.
elements.named_in: Advanced C++: Programming Styles and Idioms - James O. Coplien (1992)

elements.name: Envelope-Letter
elements.what: A handle/body variant where the envelope (handle) and letters (bodies) share a common base class, letting the letter's dynamic type change at runtime behind a stable envelope.
elements.problem: Allows an object to change its apparent class (e.g. number types promoting, state changes) while clients hold a value-semantics handle.
elements.named_in: Advanced C++: Programming Styles and Idioms - James O. Coplien (1992)

elements.name: External Polymorphism
elements.what: Make unrelated concrete classes (possibly without virtual functions or a common base) polymorphic by wrapping them in a parallel adapter hierarchy defined outside the classes.
elements.problem: Third-party or performance-critical classes cannot be modified to join an inheritance hierarchy; external polymorphism adds dynamic dispatch non-intrusively and underlies modern type erasure.
elements.named_in: External Polymorphism - Cleeland, Schmidt & Harrison (PLoP 1996)

elements.name: Typelist
elements.what: A compile-time list of types built from nested templates (or variadic packs), manipulated by metafunctions to generate code over type collections.
elements.problem: Generating hierarchies or dispatch code over an open set of types requires a compile-time collection abstraction; typelists are that data structure.
elements.named_in: Modern C++ Design - Andrei Alexandrescu (2001)
elements.borderline: Metaprogramming infrastructure rather than an end-user design mechanism; kept as the named building block of policy/hierarchy generation.

elements.name: Include Guard
elements.what: Preprocessor conditionals (or #pragma once) that make a header idempotent under multiple inclusion.
elements.problem: Multiple inclusion of a header causes redefinition errors; the guard is the established convention making header composition safe.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022); also More C++ Idioms (Wikibooks)
elements.borderline: Preprocessor mechanics at the raw-syntax floor; kept because both Fluent C and the wikibook catalog it as a named pattern.

elements.name: Execute Around Method
elements.what: A method/wrapper takes user code (block, lambda, or smart-pointer access) and runs fixed before/after actions around it - acquire/release, lock/unlock, open/close.
elements.problem: Paired pre/post obligations are easy to forget or mismatch at every call site; wrapping the user action guarantees the pairing.
elements.named_in: Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns - Kent Beck (1997)

elements.name: Opaque Pointer
elements.what: An API exposes only a forward-declared struct pointer whose definition lives in the implementation file, so clients cannot see or touch the representation.
elements.problem: C has no access control; the incomplete type makes information hiding compiler-enforced and keeps ABI stable across representation changes.
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996)

elements.name: X-Macro
elements.what: A single macro list of entries is expanded multiple times with different definitions of X to generate parallel artifacts (enums, string tables, dispatch tables) from one source of truth.
elements.problem: Parallel lists (enum + names + handlers) drift apart under maintenance; the X-macro keeps them generated from one list.
elements.named_in: The New C: X Macros - Randy Meyers, C/C++ Users Journal (2001)

elements.name: Function Pointer Dispatch Table
elements.what: An indexed or keyed table of function pointers replaces switch/if chains: look up the handler, then call it.
elements.problem: Large multiway branches are slow to extend and error-prone; a table makes dispatch data-driven, O(1), and extensible (also the substrate for state machines and command interpreters).
elements.named_in: The C Programming Language, 2nd ed. - Kernighan & Ritchie (1988), sec. 5.11 pointers to functions

elements.name: Callback with Context Pointer
elements.what: Register a function pointer together with an opaque void* context that the callee passes back on invocation, giving the callback access to its state.
elements.problem: C function pointers carry no environment; the paired context pointer emulates closures so one callback implementation can serve many registered instances.
elements.named_in: Callback (computer programming) - Wikipedia; used pervasively in Hanson's C Interfaces and Implementations (closure 'cl' parameters)

elements.name: Goto Cleanup
elements.what: On failure, jump forward to a single labeled cleanup section at the end of the function that releases resources in reverse acquisition order.
elements.problem: Multi-step acquisition in C needs unwinding on every failure path; one exit chain avoids duplicated cleanup code and leak-prone nested conditionals.
elements.named_in: Linux kernel coding style (living); also Goto Error Handling in Fluent C - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: setjmp/longjmp Structured Error Handling
elements.what: Wrap setjmp/longjmp in TRY/RAISE/EXCEPT macros to implement raise-and-unwind exception semantics in C.
elements.problem: Propagating rare deep errors through every return path clutters C code; non-local jumps deliver the error directly to a handler (at the cost of manual resource discipline).
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996), Except interface

elements.name: OO in C via Explicit Vtable
elements.what: Structs of function pointers (shared per 'class', pointed to by each instance) plus first-argument self pointers implement classes, inheritance, and dynamic dispatch in C.
elements.problem: C lacks language-level polymorphism; the explicit vtable brings substitutable implementations to drivers, OS interfaces, and embedded frameworks.
elements.named_in: Object-Oriented Programming with ANSI-C - Axel-Tobias Schreiner (1993/2011)

elements.name: First-Class ADT
elements.what: A C module whose datatype is an opaque pointer created/destroyed through the API, so multiple independent instances exist as first-class values.
elements.problem: Single-instance C modules with global state cannot be multiply instantiated or tested in isolation; the first-class ADT gives instance semantics and total information hiding.
elements.named_in: Patterns in C - Adam Tornhill (2015; earlier EuroPLoP 2005 paper)

elements.name: Return Status Code
elements.what: Functions return a numeric/enum status indicating success or a specific failure, delivering actual results through out-parameters.
elements.problem: C has no exceptions; a uniform status-return channel makes failure explicit and checkable at every call boundary.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022); also Preschern's EuroPLoP error-handling pattern papers

elements.name: Special Return Value
elements.what: Reserve one or more values of the normal return domain (NULL, -1, EOF) to signal failure in-band, avoiding a separate status channel.
elements.problem: When the result domain has spare values, in-band signaling keeps APIs terse; the C-API-convention face of the general sentinel-value element.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Samurai Principle
aka: return victorious or not at all
elements.what: For errors the caller cannot meaningfully handle, do not return an error code - assert/abort at the failure point instead.
elements.problem: Propagating unhandleable errors buries the fault and corrupts state downstream; failing fast at the point of detection preserves the evidence.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Guard Clause
aka: replace nested conditional with guard clauses
elements.what: Check preconditions/special cases at the top of a function and return immediately, keeping the main path unindented.
elements.problem: Deeply nested conditionals obscure the dominant path; guard clauses flatten control flow and make precondition handling explicit.
elements.named_in: Refactoring - Martin Fowler (1999), 'Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses'; also Fluent C (2022)
elements.borderline: Statement-level code-shaping idiom below typical design altitude; kept because two catalogs name it as a pattern.

elements.name: Aggregate Instance
elements.what: Bundle multiple related values into a struct and pass/return that aggregate by value instead of using several out-parameters.
elements.problem: Returning multiple related data items through separate pointers scatters the contract; the aggregate makes the data relationship explicit and copyable.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Out-Parameters
elements.what: Return data by writing through caller-supplied pointers, keeping the return value free for status.
elements.problem: C functions return a single value; out-parameters deliver multiple results while preserving the status-code channel.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Caller-Owned Buffer
elements.what: The caller allocates and owns the buffer, passing pointer and size for the callee to fill.
elements.problem: Callee-side allocation forces heap use and ambiguous ownership; caller-owned buffers keep allocation strategy (stack, static, pool) and lifetime with the caller - vital in embedded code.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Callee Allocates
elements.what: The callee allocates the result buffer (of size only it knows) and returns it with a paired deallocation function the caller must invoke.
elements.problem: When result size is unknown to the caller, callee allocation avoids guess-and-retry sizing at the cost of an explicit ownership-transfer contract.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: container_of
elements.what: Recover a pointer to the enclosing struct from a pointer to one of its embedded members via offsetof arithmetic, enabling intrusive/generic embedded nodes.
elements.problem: Generic subsystems (lists, kobjects, work items) hold pointers to embedded member structs; container_of maps back to the owning object without per-type containers or extra pointers.
elements.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

elements.name: Typestate
elements.what: Encode an object's protocol state in its static type (consuming and returning distinct types per transition) so illegal operations for the current state do not compile.
elements.problem: Runtime state checks catch protocol misuse only when it happens; typestate moves the state machine into the type system - idiomatic in Rust where move semantics enforce transitions.
elements.named_in: Typestate: A Programming Language Concept for Enhancing Software Reliability - Strom & Yemini, IEEE TSE (1986); Rust realization in The Embedded Rust Book

elements.name: Newtype
elements.what: Wrap an existing type in a distinct single-field type so the compiler distinguishes semantically different values (Miles vs Kilometers) and the wrapper can carry its own invariants and trait implementations.
elements.problem: Raw primitives let unrelated quantities be mixed silently and leak representation; the zero-cost wrapper restores type safety and API encapsulation.
elements.named_in: Rust Design Patterns (rust-unofficial, living); keyword-level origin in Haskell (newtype)

elements.name: Interior Mutability
elements.what: Types like Cell/RefCell/Mutex allow controlled mutation through shared (immutable) references by moving aliasing checks to runtime or hardware.
elements.problem: Rust's aliasing rules forbid mutation through shared references, but caches, counters, and observer lists need it; interior mutability provides a sound, localized escape hatch.
elements.named_in: The Rust Programming Language - Klabnik & Nichols ('RefCell<T> and the Interior Mutability Pattern')

elements.name: Sealed Trait
elements.what: A public trait made unimplementable outside its crate via an unnameable private supertrait, keeping the set of implementors closed.
elements.problem: Public traits are otherwise open to downstream implementations, so adding a method is a breaking change; sealing preserves evolvability of the API.
elements.named_in: Rust API Guidelines (C-SEALED, living)

elements.name: Static Factory Method
elements.what: A public static method returns instances instead of a public constructor, allowing naming, caching, subtype return, and non-instantiation.
elements.problem: Constructors cannot be named, cannot return cached or covariant instances, and always allocate; static factories decouple 'get an instance' from 'construct an object' (distinct from GoF Factory Method).
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2001; 3rd ed. 2018, Item 1)

elements.name: Defensive Copy
elements.what: Copy mutable inputs on receipt and mutable internal state on return, so external aliases can never mutate an object's invariant-protected state.
elements.problem: Sharing references to mutable components lets callers corrupt invariants (time-of-check/time-of-use attacks); copying at the boundary restores encapsulation.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2001; 3rd ed. Item 50)

elements.name: Dispose Pattern
elements.what: Objects owning unmanaged resources expose an explicit Dispose/close method, invoked deterministically via language constructs (using / try-with-resources), with finalizers only as backstop.
elements.problem: Garbage collection reclaims memory but not files, sockets, or handles at predictable times; the pattern restores deterministic cleanup in GC languages.
elements.named_in: Framework Design Guidelines - Cwalina & Abrams (2005); Effective Java Item 9 (try-with-resources)

elements.name: Marker Interface
elements.what: An empty interface whose only purpose is to tag implementing classes with a compile-time-checkable property (Serializable, Cloneable).
elements.problem: Some type-level properties carry no operations but must be testable and enforceable by the type system; the marker makes membership a static type.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (3rd ed., Item 41)

elements.name: Serialization Proxy
elements.what: Serialize a small dedicated proxy object representing the logical state instead of the real object, reconstructing the real object through its public constructors on read.
elements.problem: Default serialization is an extralinguistic constructor that bypasses invariant checks and locks in representation; the proxy restores invariant enforcement and representation freedom.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (3rd ed., Item 90)

elements.name: Type-Safe Enum
elements.what: Represent an enumerated type as a class with a fixed set of public static final instances and a private constructor, giving type safety, namespacing, and behavior per constant.
elements.problem: int/#define constants are unchecked, unprintable, and collide; the pattern (since absorbed into Java enum / C++ enum class) makes enumerations real types. Bloch's enum-singleton is a folded application.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (1st ed. 2001, Item 21)

elements.name: Double-Checked Locking
elements.what: Check a lazily-initialized field once without the lock, and only on apparent-null acquire the lock and check again before initializing.
elements.problem: Locking on every access to initialized-once state is costly; the idiom skips the lock on the hot path - famously unsound without memory-model support (volatile/atomics).
elements.named_in: Double-Checked Locking: An Optimization Pattern for Efficiently Initializing and Accessing Thread-safe Objects - Schmidt & Harrison (PLoP 1996); POSA2

parked_architecture.name: Abstraction Layer / Hardware Abstraction Layer (Fluent C, Beningo)
parked_architecture.why: Fluent C names 'Abstraction Layer' for escaping #ifdef variant hell, but as a platform-spanning layer it states component/system structure - architecture realm (HAL).

parked_architecture.name: Self-Contained Component (Fluent C, Organizing Files chapter)
parked_architecture.why: Prescribes directory/component structure and dependency direction across modules - code-organization at component granularity, feeds the architecture catalog.

excluded_notable.name: Enum singleton (Effective Java Item 3)
excluded_notable.why: Folded per charter: an implementation note on the GoF Singleton element, not a separate mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Safe bool idiom
excluded_notable.why: Established C++ idiom (wikibooks) but obsoleted by C++11 explicit operator bool; historical language-workaround, recorded not cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: nullptr idiom / Address Of / Checked Delete / Multi-statement Macro / Named Loop (wikibooks)
excluded_notable.why: Micro-idioms or workarounds superseded by language features; below design altitude.

excluded_notable.name: Barton-Nackman trick
excluded_notable.why: Historical CRTP application (folded into CRTP note per one-element-per-mechanism rule).

excluded_notable.name: errno convention
excluded_notable.why: Library/ABI convention rather than a design mechanism; noted as related convention under Return Status Code.

excluded_notable.name: Rust micro-idioms (mem::take/replace, temporary mutability, on-stack dynamic dispatch, format! concatenation)
excluded_notable.why: Named in rust-unofficial/patterns but statement-level usage tips below design altitude.

excluded_notable.name: struct hack / flexible array member
excluded_notable.why: Raw language feature (C99) rather than a named design mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Fluent C memory patterns (Stack First, Eternal Memory, Memory Pool, Allocation Wrapper, Pointer Check, Dedicated Ownership)
excluded_notable.why: Deliberately left to the resource-management scout to avoid duplicate ownership; Memory Pool = object pool/memory arena family. Recorded so they are not lost if that scout misses Fluent C.

excluded_notable.name: Fluent C iterator patterns (Index Access, Cursor Iterator, Callback Iterator)
excluded_notable.why: C-API realizations of GoF Iterator; fold as implementation notes under Iterator rather than separate mechanisms.

notes: Coverage: C++ 29 elements (wikibooks More C++ Idioms fetched live and swept; Coplien 1992, Alexandrescu 2001, Sutter, Meyers, Iglberger, Core Guidelines drawn on), C 17 (Hanson, Schreiner, Tornhill, Preschern Fluent C ch.1-4 pattern names confirmed via live search of the O'Reilly ToC, kernel style, K&R, LDD3), Rust 4 (rust-unofficial/patterns SUMMARY.md and Rust API Guidelines C-SEALED fetched live), Java/.NET 7 (Effective Java, Framework Design Guidelines). Deliberate charter compliance: RAII guard folded into raii aka; COW string folded into copy-on-write; handle/body folded into pimpl; enum singleton folded out. Dedup risks flagged for the merger: copy-on-write, double-checked-locking, mixin, guard-clause and special-return-value may collide with concurrency/error-handling/general scouts - kept per over-inclusion rule. Thin spots: Python/JS/Go idioms out of charter (context manager, decorator-as-idiom, goroutine idioms unswept); Coplien's algebraic-hierarchy and other exotic 1992 idioms omitted as low-recurrence; wikibooks micro-idioms (attorney-client, base-from-member, member detector, non-throwing swap) intentionally not enumerated individually - one further pass over that list could add ~5-8 borderline micro-idioms.
